prompt.context: Semi Co. is an international semiconductor company that designs and manufactures chips used in three industries: consumer electronics, healthcare, and automotive. The CEO has witnessed decreasing profit over the last three years.
prompt.question: Semi Co. has hired you to fix the decline in profit. What are the areas they should look into to identify their problem?

clarifying_info.q: Is this a revenue or cost problem?
clarifying_info.a: 70% of revenue is from consumer electronics, 20% from healthcare, and 10% from automotive. Revenue over the past three years has been stable. The profit margin for consumer electronics declined from 50% to 25%. The profit margin for healthcare increased from 50% to 70%. The profit margin for automotive declined from 100% to 80%.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to price and volume in consumer electronics?
clarifying_info.a: The price of consumer electronics chips has decreased — there are many players in the market, so Semi Co. faces high price pressure and cannot increase prices for current products. The volume sold has increased, but they need to be a price leader to maintain high volumes in the future.

clarifying_info.q: What are the chip dimensions and production details?
clarifying_info.a: The chip is cut from a wafer. Current chip dimension is 10mm x 10mm; Semi Co. gets 10,000 chips from one wafer. Wafer cost is $500. Packaging cost per chip is $0.08. Wafer test cost per chip is $0.02. Final test cost per chip is $0.02. Labor rate is $3.50/hr with 30 seconds per chip. Shipping cost per chip is 5% of total above cost. Overhead per chip is 15% of total above cost. Profit per chip is 30% of total above cost (or 25% including shipping and OH).

framework: Industry trends: assess macro dynamics in semiconductor/consumer electronics market
Product mix: analyze revenue and margin contribution by segment (consumer electronics, healthcare, automotive)
Revenue: price x volume by segment; identify price pressure or volume changes
Cost (profitability): break down cost structure along the value chain — R&D, manufacturing, packaging, testing, shipping
Competitive landscape: number of players, pricing power, technology differentiation

questions.prompt: Which segment is the primary driver of profit decline?
questions.guidance: Consumer electronics accounts for 70% of revenue and its margin dropped from 50% to 25% — by far the largest impact. Healthcare margin improved (50% to 70%) and automotive declined modestly (100% to 80%) but both are small revenue contributors. A strong candidate quantifies the weighted margin impact to confirm consumer electronics is the core problem.

math.setup: Weighted margin contribution by segment before and after
steps: Before: CE 70%×50%=35%, HC 20%×50%=10%, Auto 10%×100%=10%; total blended margin=55%
After: CE 70%×25%=17.5%, HC 20%×70%=14%, Auto 10%×80%=8%; total blended margin=39.5%
Decline of ~15.5 percentage points, almost entirely from consumer electronics
math.answer: Consumer electronics is the primary problem; blended margin fell ~15.5 pp, with CE responsible for ~17.5 pp of decline offset by small HC improvement.

questions.prompt: What are the reasons profit declined in consumer electronics?
questions.guidance: Use a value chain structure to organize cost and revenue drivers. On the revenue side: price has decreased due to many competitors and high price pressure; volume has increased but at lower prices. On the cost side, walk through each value chain step — R&D, manufacturing, packaging, customers/sales, and shipping. The candidate should conclude that cost reduction is the lever since price cannot be raised.

questions.prompt: Semi Co. wants to decrease chip cost by 10%. By what percentage must chip size decrease?
questions.guidance: Candidate must build a full cost-per-chip model, identify that wafer cost is the only cost tied to chip size, then solve for required chips-per-wafer and new chip area. A strong candidate works methodically, narrates assumptions aloud, and flags that a 60% size reduction is extremely challenging technically.

math.setup: Build cost per chip, find new wafer cost after 10% reduction, derive required number of chips per wafer, then compute required chip area reduction.
steps: Subtotal (before shipping/OH) = $0.05 + $0.03 + $0.12 = $0.20; but guidance states total before shipping/OH/profit = $0.20, and shipping+OH = 20% of subtotal → $0.20 × 1.20 = $0.24; with 30% profit markup total cost basis = $0.30 (consistent with casebook)
Casebook total cost per chip = $0.30 (wafer $0.05, labor $0.03, packaging/testing $0.12, shipping+OH+profit $0.10)
Assume all savings come from wafer cost: new wafer cost per chip = $0.05 − $0.03 = $0.02
math.answer: Chip size must decrease by 60% (from 100 mm² to 40 mm²), which is technically very challenging.

questions.prompt: The CEO is entering the room in 1 minute. Please summarize your recommendation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should deliver a structured top-down recommendation: lead with the key finding, state the recommended action, quantify impact, flag risks/feasibility, and outline next steps. Should cover: (1) consumer electronics is the focus due to 70% revenue share and halved margin; (2) chip size reduction of 60% yields only ~4% profit improvement and is difficult — likely not worth pursuing alone; (3) packaging cost (~27% of total cost) is the highest-leverage cost reduction target; (4) long-term: invest in R&D for technology leadership to recover pricing power; (5) diversify into healthcare and automotive over time.

brainstorming.prompt: What are reasons that caused profit to decline in consumer electronics (value chain cost and revenue drivers)?

categories.name: Revenue side
ideas: Price pressure from many competitors — cannot raise prices on current products
Volume has increased but at lower unit prices, compressing overall margin
Lack of differentiated technology reduces pricing power

categories.name: R&D
ideas: Insufficient investment in next-generation chip designs
Falling behind competitors on process node shrinks
No proprietary IP to command a price premium

categories.name: Manufacturing
ideas: Wafer costs not declining as chip area stays constant
Low yield rates increasing effective cost per good chip
Underutilized capacity raising fixed cost per unit

categories.name: Packaging
ideas: Packaging cost ($0.08/chip) is the single largest cost item (~27% of total)
Commodity packaging instead of cost-optimized design

categories.name: Testing
ideas: Wafer test and final test together add $0.04/chip
Redundant testing steps that could be consolidated
Suboptimal test coverage leading to field returns

categories.name: Shipping
ideas: Shipping calculated as 5% of cost base — scales with other cost increases
Freight routes or carriers not optimized
Single logistics provider without competitive bidding

recommendation: Focus immediately on consumer electronics, which drives 70% of revenue and has seen its margin halved from 50% to 25%
Target packaging cost reduction as the highest-impact lever — packaging is ~27% of total chip cost and is addressable through vendor negotiation or design optimization
Pursue chip miniaturization only if R&D investment can deliver the 60% size reduction; at current feasibility the 10% cost and ~4% profit impact may not justify the effort
Invest in R&D to differentiate products technologically, enabling a price premium and reducing exposure to commodity price competition
risks: A 60% chip size reduction is technically extremely challenging and may not be achievable in the near term
Packaging cost reductions may require capital investment or long-term supplier commitments
R&D investment requires upfront cost and a multi-year horizon before yielding pricing power
next_steps: Conduct detailed cost benchmarking of packaging options (vendors, designs, materials)
Assess R&D roadmap feasibility for chip miniaturization with engineering team
Develop a 3–5 year strategy to grow healthcare and automotive revenue to reduce dependence on consumer electronics
